# What to Submit: Your Final Deliverables

By Phase V, you've done serious research. Now it's time to share it. The final submission for this course has two parts: a **PDF report** and a **live GitHub Pages website**. This page explains exactly what each one is, what goes in it, and how to make sure you haven't missed anything.

---

## The Two Final Outputs

| | PDF Report | GitHub Pages Website |
|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | A formatted research document | A public website with your portfolio |
| **Rendered from** | Your `.qmd` file with `format: pdf` | Your `.qmd` file(s) with `format: html` |
| **Audience** | Academic (instructor, peers) | Public (potential employers, classmates) |
| **Submitted how** | Uploaded to Blackboard or emailed | URL submitted — the site itself is the submission |
| **Contains** | Full report with citations, tables, figures | Same content, plus your research process and vault highlights |

Both documents are produced from the same Quarto files — you just render them with different format settings.

---

## Part 1: The PDF Report

Your PDF report is a complete research document. Think of it as something you could submit to a class or show a future employer as a writing sample.

### Required Sections

Your report must include all of the following sections, in this order:

::: {.callout-important}
## Required Report Sections

- [ ] **Title page** — Title, your name, course name, date
- [ ] **Abstract** — 150–200 words summarizing the study (what you asked, how you studied it, what you found)
- [ ] **Introduction** — Background, why this topic matters, your research questions
- [ ] **Method** — How you collected your data, what your codebook measured, how many units you analyzed
- [ ] **Results** — What you found (tables, figures, frequencies — the numbers)
- [ ] **Discussion** — What the results mean, how they connect to existing research, limitations
- [ ] **References** — APA-formatted bibliography (Zotero can generate this automatically)
:::

### Rendering to PDF

In your `.qmd` file's header, set:

```yaml
---
title: "Your Report Title"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format: pdf
---
```

Then click **Render** in RStudio. The PDF will appear in your project folder and open automatically.

::: {.callout-tip}
## PDF Rendering Requires a LaTeX Installation

If you see an error like `"xelatex not found"` when rendering to PDF, you need to install TinyTeX. Run this once in the RStudio Console:

```r
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
```

This takes about 5 minutes. After it completes, restart RStudio and try rendering again.
:::

---

## Part 2: The GitHub Pages Website

Your GitHub Pages site is a live, public-facing version of your research portfolio. It's hosted at a URL like:

```
https://yourusername.github.io/your-repo-name/
```

### What the Site Should Include

Your portfolio website should contain:

::: {.callout-important}
## Required Website Pages

- [ ] **Home/index page** — Brief introduction: who you are, what this project is
- [ ] **Research summary** — Your main findings explained in plain language (not jargon)
- [ ] **Full report** — Either embedded or linked as a downloadable PDF
- [ ] **About** — A short bio and links to your GitHub profile
:::

The site doesn't need to be elaborate. A clean, readable site with working links is better than an ambitious design that's broken.

### What a Finished Portfolio Looks Like

::: {.callout-note}
## Screenshot Placeholder

*[Screenshot: Example student portfolio showing a homepage with a research project title, brief abstract, navigation links to the full report and methods section, and a simple header with the student's name. The site uses the default Quarto cosmo theme with readable fonts and good contrast.]*

A finished portfolio typically has a simple navigation bar at the top, a clear headline for the project, and 2–3 paragraphs describing what you studied and what you found — written for a general audience, not an academic one.
:::

### Publishing to GitHub Pages

1. Render your Quarto site (it outputs to the `docs/` folder)
2. Commit and push all files to GitHub
3. In your GitHub repository, go to **Settings → Pages**
4. Set the source to **"Deploy from a branch"**, branch: `main`, folder: `/docs`
5. Click Save. Your site will be live within a few minutes.

After publishing, test every link on your site in a browser (not just in RStudio's preview).

---

## Side-by-Side Comparison

| Section | PDF Report | GitHub Pages Site |
|---|---|---|
| Title & Author | ✅ Title page | ✅ On homepage |
| Abstract | ✅ Formal abstract | ✅ Rewritten for general audience |
| Introduction | ✅ Full academic intro | Optional (brief version) |
| Method | ✅ Full methodology | Optional (brief summary) |
| Results | ✅ Tables + figures | ✅ Key figures, plain language |
| Discussion | ✅ Full discussion | ✅ "What we found" in plain language |
| References | ✅ Full APA bibliography | Optional (link to PDF) |
| Process notes | ❌ Not included | Optional (can add a "process" page) |

---

## Final Submission Checklist

Use this before you submit anything:

### PDF Report
- [ ] All required sections are present and in order
- [ ] Research questions are stated clearly in the Introduction
- [ ] Method section explains your codebook and sample
- [ ] Results section contains at least one table or figure
- [ ] Discussion answers your original research questions
- [ ] References are in APA format
- [ ] PDF renders without errors

### GitHub Pages Site
- [ ] Site is live and accessible at a public URL
- [ ] Homepage clearly states your name and project
- [ ] All navigation links work when accessed from the live URL
- [ ] Report is either embedded or downloadable
- [ ] Site renders correctly on mobile (check on your phone)
- [ ] You've submitted the URL, not just the GitHub repository link

---

## Common Last-Minute Problems

**"My PDF renders locally but not on GitHub"**
GitHub Pages only hosts HTML — the PDF is a separate file you produce locally and then push to the repository. Make sure the PDF is committed to your `docs/` folder.

**"My charts look fine in RStudio but are missing in the PDF"**
Check that your code chunks that produce plots use `echo: false` if you don't want the code shown, and make sure the chunk is not set to `eval: false`. Also ensure ggplot2 is loaded.

**"My GitHub Pages site is showing a 404 error"**
Check that (1) the `/docs` folder exists and contains an `index.html`, and (2) GitHub Pages is configured to serve from `/docs` on the `main` branch. It can take up to 10 minutes for changes to go live.

**"I don't know if I need the full PDF in the website"**
You should have both. The PDF is the academic deliverable. The website is the portfolio. Link to your PDF from the website so visitors can download it.
